title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) emerged shortly after the introduction of methicillin in 1959, transforming from an isolated laboratory finding into a global health challenge. Defined by the presence of the mecA or mecC gene within the staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCCmec), MRSA demonstrates resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics through altered penicillin-binding proteins that maintain cell wall synthesis despite antimicrobial pressure. This course reviews the evolution of MRSA into hospital- and community-associated forms and their differing clinical features (ranging from mild skin lesions to life-threatening conditions), molecular biology, antibiotic susceptibility, and treatment. The emergence of vancomycin-intermediate and -resistant strains and the urgency of continued surveillance and therapeutic innovation are also discussed.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Introduction
content: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection is one of the leading causes of hospital-acquired infections and is commonly associated with significant morbidity, mortality, increased length of stay, and a high cost burden. [1] Soon after methicillin entered clinical use in 1959, Professor Patricia Jevons identified methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) in 1960. In February 1961, The British Medical Journal published her observation of this resistant strain, now recognized as MRSA. The pathogen rapidly established endemicity in hospitals across the United Kingdom and, over time, expanded into a widespread global health concern.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Introduction
content: MRSA is defined by the presence of the 20 to 65 kb staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCC mec) element inserted within the orfX (an RNA methyltransferase) gene of S aureus . SCC mec contains the mecA gene complex (responsible for methicillin resistance) and a set of site-specific recombinase genes ( ccrA and ccrB ) responsible for its mobility. [2] Oxacillin is a derivative of methicillin and is used to test for MRSA. Because of methicillin's historic role, we still use the acronym MRSA to describe these isolates.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Introduction
content: MRSA carries the mecA and mecC genes, which confer oxacillin resistance by encoding a different penicillin-binding protein (PBP) that allows cell wall synthesis in the presence of beta-lactams due to low affinity for binding. According to the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI), MRSA is defined as isolates with a methicillin minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 4 μg/mL or greater or an oxacillin MIC of greater than 2 μg/mL. The mecA gene was first identified in Japan in 1987. The discovery of mecC in 2011 (in England) was significant because it represented a new mechanism of methicillin resistance in MRSA, distinct from the more common mecA gene.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Introduction
content: MRSA infections can be further divided into hospital-associated (HA-MRSA) and community-associated (CA-MRSA) infections, which differ not only in their clinical features and molecular biology but also in their antibiotic susceptibility and treatment. [3] [4] Consequently, MRSA represents a significant challenge in modern infectious disease management. Furthermore, the ongoing emergence of vancomycin-intermediate and -resistant strains further underscores the need for vigilant diagnosis, antimicrobial stewardship, and evidence-based therapeutic strategies to mitigate resistance and improve outcomes.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Etiology
content: MRSA are strains of S aureus that have developed resistance to beta-lactam and many other antibiotics. MRSA strains are transmitted by direct skin-to-skin contact as well as indirect contact of surfaces. MRSA is not inherently more virulent than methicillin-sensitive S aureus . Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Staphylococcus aureus Infections ," for further information.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Epidemiology
content: The history of MRSA infection dates back to 1961, when the organism was first described. Since that time, the incidence and prevalence of MRSA infections have risen dramatically. Recent population-based studies have suggested a reduction in hospital-acquired MRSA (HA-MRSA) incidence within the United States, although this improvement was at the expense of a growing prevalence of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA). Reported MRSA infection rates range from 7% to 60%. [5] Until the 1990s, MRSA primarily affected individuals with healthcare exposure, but subsequent cases began appearing among people with no prior hospitalization, leading to the classification of MRSA into hospital-acquired and community-acquired forms. Globally, MRSA incidence rose sharply throughout the 1990s and peaked around 2005. In the United States, HA-MRSA rates declined by 17.1% from 2005 to 2012, [6] likely due to improved adherence to infection control measures. The rate of decline slowed from 2013 to 2016, while CA-MRSA showed a modest increase between 2012 and 2017. [7]

content: Staphylococcus aureus commonly colonizes the nares, followed by the oropharynx, skin, and gastrointestinal tract. In intensive care settings, the rectum and throat serve as the primary sites of MRSA colonization. Among carriers, nasal strains most frequently cause subsequent infection, and nasal carriers face a 5-fold greater risk of healthcare-associated infection than noncarriers. title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Pathophysiology -- Antibiotic Resistance
content: The primary reason for MRSA resistance to semisynthetic antistaphylococcal penicillins is due to the presence of the mecA gene sequence, which is known to generate transpeptidase PB2a, lowering the organism's affinity to bind to beta-lactam antibiotics. [4] The mecA gene sequence is located on a mobile chromosomal element termed SCCmec . [3]

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Pathophysiology -- Antibiotic Resistance
content: The term vancomycin-intermediate S aureus (VISA)  is confusing for several reasons. Initially, VISA can appear susceptible when tested with routine laboratory methods. However, clinical isolates with phenotypes identified as having a vancomycin MIC of <2 µg/mL contain subpopulations with higher MICs. These subpopulations are capable of growing in the presence of various concentrations of vancomycin (eg, <2 µg/mL to 8 µg/mL) and are termed heterogeneous or heteroresistant vancomycin-intermediate S aureus (hVISA). [13]

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Pathophysiology -- Antibiotic Resistance
content: The CLSI designates the intermediate breakpoint range for VISA as 4 to 8 µg/mL. However, the EUCAST does not use an intermediate S aureus classification; instead, strains with breakpoints greater than 2 µg/mL are considered resistant in their classification scheme. Both hVISA and VISA strains emerge from multiple mutations driven by prolonged vancomycin treatment. [15] Many authors believe that hVISA is a precursor of VISA. Disc diffusion methods are unreliable at identifying hVISA and VISA, and agar or broth dilution methods are recommended on that basis.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Pathophysiology -- Cell wall structures
content: Capsular polysaccharides enhance the virulence of S aureus by impairing antibody-mediated opsonization, complement activation, and phagocytosis. Staphylococcal protein A (surface-associated protein) is a cell wall structure that protects the microorganism from phagocytosis by attaching to the circulating IgG. Cell-surface clumping factor molecules initiate S aureus -fibrinogen adherence.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Pathophysiology -- Extracellular toxins
content: MRSA expresses alpha, beta, gamma, and delta (hemolysin) toxins. Among these toxins, alpha toxin is considered a major virulence factor. [18] Staphylococcal enterotoxins A, B, C, D, and E are the main virulence factors in human food poisoning; these are pyrogenic exotoxins belonging to S aureus superantigens. These bacterial enterotoxins stimulate IL-4 and IL-10 expression, leading to the activation of TH2 cells and subsequently suppressing the clearance of invading microorganisms.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Pathophysiology -- Extracellular toxins
content: Panton-Valentine leucocidin (PVL) is a potent exotoxin produced by MRSA. [19] PVL targets and destroys the plasma membranes of polymorphonuclear cells. Additionally, PVL stimulates these cells to release reactive oxygen species, interleukin 8, and lysozymes, as well as triggering histamine release from basophils. Toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST) is one of the most potent antigens produced by S aureus and is implicated in toxic shock syndrome in humans. This disease occurs when TSST is released, triggering the production of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin 1 (IL-1), and interleukin 2 (IL-2). Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins are serine proteases that cause staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and bullous impetigo. Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins destroy the desmoglein-1 protein, causing damage to the epidermis.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Pathophysiology -- Extracellular enzymes
content: MRSA causes plasma coagulation by releasing the coagulase (Coa) enzyme. Additionally, the Coa enzyme contains a D1D2 domain that specifically binds prothrombin. Staphylokinase is an extracellular enzyme that activates plasminogen, leading to fibrin clot lysis and subsequent bacterial propagation. Consequently, MRSA strains that produce staphylokinase typically exhibit reduced biofilm development in both in vitro and noninvasive human infections. Staphylococcal nucleases are heat-stable, calcium-dependent enzymes that destroy DNA and RNA substrates. Staphylococcal proteases help bacteria disseminate by evading the host defense. Staphylococcus aureus hyaluronidase facilitates bacterial migration by degrading hyaluronic acid in the extracellular matrix and biofilms. [20]

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- History and Physical
content: MRSA can cause a range of organ-specific infections, the most common being the skin and subcutaneous tissues, followed by invasive infections like bacteremia, osteomyelitis, meningitis, pneumonia, lung abscess, and empyema. Infective endocarditis caused by MRSA is associated with increased morbidity and mortality compared to any other organism. People who inject drugs are at particularly high risk for MRSA endocarditis.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- History and Physical -- Skin and Soft Tissue Infections
content: CA-MRSA is a predominant organism associated with skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs), eg, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, and diabetic foot ulcers. CA-MRSA is also increasingly associated with more invasive diseases than those not due to MRSA. More frequently, these infections are multidrug-resistant, leading to frequent recurrence, increased hospitalization, and mortality. [6] CA-MRSA is a common cause of skin lesions that are often incorrectly attributed to spider bites. title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- History and Physical -- Bone and joint infection
content: Staphylococci are the most common cause of bone and joint infections. MRSA can cause osteomyelitis of the spine and long bones of the upper and lower extremities by extension of local infection from a wound or as a part of a hematogenous infection. Similarly, MRSA can cause septic arthritis of both native and prosthetic joints. [22] Please see StatPearls' companion resources, " Septic Arthritis ," " Septic Arthritis of the Pediatric Hip ," " Septic Bursitis ," " Osteomyelitis ," " Vertebral Osteomyelitis ," and " Periprosthetic Joint Infections ," for additional details.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- History and Physical -- Pneumonia
content: Staphylococcal pneumonia, historically known as postinfluenza pneumonia, was a distinct clinical entity with a dramatic onset of respiratory symptoms and mortality ranging from 80% to 90% in the preantibiotic era. The condition carried specific radiological features, including cavitary lesions, empyema, and pyopneumothorax, as well as pathological features, eg, pulmonary hemorrhage and microabscess formation.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- History and Physical -- Pneumonia
content: In the postantibiotic period, the course has been less explosive, not always associated with viral influenza, related to other risk factors for S aureus infections, and carries a mortality of around 30% to 40%. Nevertheless, CA-MRSA, causing life-threatening necrotizing pneumonia in otherwise healthy individuals, has been reported across the United States recently. [23] Necrotizing pneumonia is characterized by severe respiratory symptoms, high fevers, hemoptysis, and hypotension, and rapidly progresses to sepsis and septic shock with leukopenia and elevated C-reactive protein. Multilobar cavitating alveolar infiltrates in this clinical setting are consistent with CA-MRSA infection.

In the postantibiotic period, the course has been less explosive, not always associated with viral influenza, related to other risk factors for S aureus infections, and carries a mortality of around 30% to 40%. Nevertheless, CA-MRSA, causing life-threatening necrotizing pneumonia in otherwise healthy individuals, has been reported across the United States recently. [23] Necrotizing pneumonia is characterized by severe respiratory symptoms, high fevers, hemoptysis, and hypotension, and rapidly progresses to sepsis and septic shock with leukopenia and elevated C-reactive protein. Multilobar cavitating alveolar infiltrates in this clinical setting are consistent with CA-MRSA infection.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- History and Physical -- Pneumonia
content: MRSA is also a leading cause of hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia. Hospital-acquired pneumonia, or nosocomial pneumonia, is characterized as pneumonia developing 48 hours or more after hospital admission, indicating that this condition was not incubating at the time of admission. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is defined as pneumonia developing 48 hours or more after implementation of endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation, and was not present before intubation. The microbiological etiology of these conditions is similar and carries a grave prognosis associated with poor overall outcomes. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Staphylococcal Pneumonia ," for additional details.

content: Bacteremia due to S aureus has been reported to be associated with mortality rates of 15% to 60%. title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- History and Physical -- Endocarditis
content: MRSA is a significant cause of bacterial endocarditis, which carries a mortality rate of between 30% and 37%. Right-sided MRSA endocarditis is commonly associated with intravenous drug use and intravenous catheters. Patients with tricuspid valve vegetations may have septic pulmonary emboli, which cause nodular infiltrates and cavitating lesions in the lungs. Similarly, patients with involvement of the mitral and aortic valves may have secondary infections in distant foci, eg, bones and joints, the kidneys, the brain, and other organs. Obtaining a history and thoroughly examining these patients is important, combined with the necessary laboratory studies and radiological tests. [24] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Endocarditis ," " Endocarditis Antibiotic Regimens ," " Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis ," and " Cardiac Abscess " for additional details.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- History and Physical -- Meningitis
content: Meningitis is defined by isolation of MRSA in 1 or more cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) or blood cultures, with signs and symptoms of acute meningitis and typical CSF findings, eg, pleocytosis (>10 cells/μL), decreased glucose level (<0.40 mg/dL), or increased protein concentration (>0.45 mg/dL). Meningitis can result from metastatic bloodstream infection or from direct extension from a postoperative wound. Furthermore, MRSA meningitis is associated with high mortality (10%-45%). This condition usually presents with altered mental status, rapid onset of fever, meningeal signs, and headache. Rarely do patients present with focal neurological deficits and seizures. [25] Please see StatPearls' companion resources, " Epidural Abscess ," " Brain Abscess ," and " Bacterial Meningitis " for further information.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Evaluation
content: When evaluating patients with presumptive or proven MRSA infection, clinicians should consider the following general questions: Does the patient have risk factors for MRSA? In the absence of risk factors, are there features of the infection that suggest MRSA may be the etiology? Is the infection limited to a single anatomic site, or has it disseminated to other sites? Does the patient have co-morbidities or socioeconomic factors that will impact the choice of antibiotic treatment? What are the potential benefits and risks of the chosen antibiotic and possible surgical option? Once the current MRSA infection has been successfully treated, what strategies can be used to reduce the risk of recurrent MRSA infections?

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Evaluation
content: Clinical suspicion in patients with risk factors for MRSA infection is crucial for diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. However, confirmation of MRSA infection should not delay treatment with empiric MRSA antibiotics. Clinicians should submit samples from suspected sources of infection for analysis, including blood, sputum, urine, wounds, CSF, and surgical specimens. [26] A Gram stain demonstrating the presence of Gram-positive cocci in clusters is suggestive of S aureus. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for MRSA identification is a valuable, rapid test while awaiting culture confirmation. [10]

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Treatment / Management -- Skin and Soft Tissue Infections
content: Superficial infections, eg, impetigo, are treated with gentle soap and water cleansing followed by topical mupirocin. For most uncomplicated SSTIs, empirical treatment is with oral antibiotics, eg, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, tetracyclines (eg, doxycycline or minocycline), or clindamycin. Higher doses of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg, 1 tablet 3 times daily or 2 tablets twice daily in adults are recommended for MRSA in patients with normal renal function. Newer agents, eg, linezolid, tedizolid, and delafloxacin, can also be used as alternative oral regimens if available and deemed cost-effective. Parenteral antibiotics are indicated for invasive SSTIs or with signs of systemic involvement, inadequate response to oral therapy, or if an SSTI occurs adjacent to an indwelling device.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Treatment / Management -- Skin and Soft Tissue Infections
content: Intravenous vancomycin is the drug of choice for most MRSA infections in hospitalized patients. This agent can be used as empiric and definitive therapy, as most MRSA infections are susceptible to vancomycin. As noted above, some sporadic cases of hVISA, VISA, and VRSA infections may not respond to glycopeptide antibiotics. The dosage depends on the type and severity of the infection. Vancomycin trough is obtained just before the fourth dose to ascertain a therapeutic level. The goal trough range is typically between 10 and 20 µg/mL. For complicated infections, the goal is 15 to 20 µg/mL. The dose should be adjusted based on serum trough levels or AUC/MIC and according to renal function.

content: Daptomycin is a suitable parenteral alternative when vancomycin is unavailable or not tolerated. Other short-acting options include ceftaroline and telavancin. Long-acting treatment options include dalbavancin and oritavancin. Regardless of the initial empiric antibiotic choice, subsequent therapy should be tailored based on the careful review of culture and susceptibility data. The duration of therapy for MRSA SSTIs typically ranges from 5 to 14 days, depending on the extent of the infection and the response to treatment.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Treatment / Management -- Bacteremia
content: Vancomycin and daptomycin are considered the standard of care according to the 2011 Infectious Diseases Society of America guidelines. [35] However, since the establishment of the guidelines, mortality due to MRSA bacteremia has not significantly changed, and remains between 20% to 30%. [36] Efforts to improve therapeutic response have led to the investigation of combination glycopeptide plus beta-lactam treatment in patients with MRSA bacteremia. Vancomycin and daptomycin, combined with a variety of beta-lactams, have generally demonstrated a shorter duration of bacteremia than the glycopeptide alone. Impact on mortality has met with mixed results; some studies demonstrate a reduction, others demonstrate no effect, and still others raise concern for increased risk due to the development of acute kidney injury in the patients receiving the antibiotic combination. [37] While additional studies are needed to establish safety, efficacy, and reduction in mortality, the use of combination antibiotic therapy should be considered for high-risk patients and those with refractory bacteremia. When to initiate combination therapy and for how long remains to be determined. However, it has been suggested that induction with combination antibiotics, followed by streamlining to monotherapy, makes biological sense. [37] Which combinations and which patient population to target are areas of unresolved but great interest.

content: Teicoplanin is a bacteriostatic glycopeptide with a similar spectrum of activity and efficacy as vancomycin and is better tolerated than vancomycin. However, teicoplanin is used less commonly due to its limited availability. title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Treatment / Management -- Endocarditis
content: The 2015 American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines recommend intravenous vancomycin as the first-line treatment for endocarditis. For patients who can neither tolerate vancomycin nor achieve adequate dosing, intravenous daptomycin is an alternative option. The recommended duration of therapy for native valve endocarditis is 6 weeks. Prosthetic valve endocarditis secondary to MRSA should be treated with intravenous vancomycin and rifampin for 6 weeks, and gentamicin should be given in the first 2 weeks of therapy. However, evidence of additional benefit of combining rifampin or gentamicin with vancomycin or daptomycin for native valve endocarditis is absent. Combination glycopeptide plus beta-lactams, telavancin, ceftaroline, and quinupristin-dalfopristin have been successfully used as salvage therapy in select patient groups. Clindamycin or linezolid should not be used to treat endocarditis because they have poorer outcomes than cell-wall-active agents, eg, vancomycin and daptomycin. [24]

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Treatment / Management -- Pneumonia
content: For MRSA pneumonia, the recommended antibiotics are vancomycin (IV), linezolid (oral/IV at a dosage of 600 mg twice daily), or clindamycin 600 mg 3 times daily if the strain is susceptible. Avoiding daptomycin is crucial because this agent is inactivated by surfactant. [38] Additionally, tigecycline is associated with an increased risk of mortality and should be used only as a last resort. [39] Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole have been used off-label in the treatment of pneumonia due to MRSA. [40] [41]

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Treatment / Management -- Salvage Therapy
content: Clinicians will encounter complicated MRSA infections that, for reasons of resistance or patient intolerance, are not amenable to treatment with standard-of-care antibiotics. It is unlikely that robust randomized clinical trials capable of evaluating the efficacy and safety of all possible antibiotic combinations that could be used to treat patients failing current therapy will be conducted. A myriad of case reports and case series that have utilized various antibiotic combinations to treat complicated MRSA infections have been published, and most report varying degrees of success. However, one must be cautious in drawing inferences due to the possibility of publication bias (ie, cases with negative outcomes often go unreported). Notwithstanding, salvage therapy using antibiotic combinations should be considered. These novel treatment approaches should be based on sound microbiological and pharmacological principles in the context of the specific MRSA strain resistance pattern and the infected host's characteristics. title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of MRSA infection depends on the anatomical sites involved, the patient's general health, source control, and the prompt administration of active antibiotics at therapeutic doses. Superficial skin infections are usually easily managed. Deep tissue infections can lead to fasciitis and require debridement in addition to antibiotics. Endovascular infections, including endocarditis, are always complicated and potentially life-threatening. Infections involving implanted medical devices and prostheses are complicated, often require removal of the implant, and prolonged courses of antibiotics. Mortality due to S aureus bacteremia is in the range of 15% to 30%. The risk of death from an MRSA infection is highest among nursing home residents, older adults, individuals with liver or kidney disease, immunocompromised hosts, and patients with severe sepsis. Adherence to quality-of-care indicators for patients with MRSA bacteremia is most important to reduce mortality. [34]

Superficial skin infections are usually easily managed. Deep tissue infections can lead to fasciitis and require debridement in addition to antibiotics. Endovascular infections, including endocarditis, are always complicated and potentially life-threatening. Infections involving implanted medical devices and prostheses are complicated, often require removal of the implant, and prolonged courses of antibiotics. Mortality due to S aureus bacteremia is in the range of 15% to 30%. The risk of death from an MRSA infection is highest among nursing home residents, older adults, individuals with liver or kidney disease, immunocompromised hosts, and patients with severe sepsis. Adherence to quality-of-care indicators for patients with MRSA bacteremia is most important to reduce mortality. [34]

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients should be educated about the ease of MRSA transmission through contact and strategies to prevent colonization and infection. In particular, adherence to hand hygiene practices, avoidance of sharing personal hygiene items, and environmental cleaning should be stressed. People who inject drugs are at very high risk of acquiring complicated MRSA infections and should receive treatment for opioid use disorder. Education efforts should address the misconception that spider bites cause what is, in reality, likely to be an MRSA skin infection. Infection control practices, including hand hygiene, should be taught and enforced at all healthcare settings.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Prevention and control of MRSA infections include essential infection-control measures, eg, strict hand hygiene and adequate contact precautions. Hand hygiene means washing hands with soap and water or an alcohol-based cleanser before and after contact with patients with MRSA. Contact precautions include the use of gowns, gloves, and possibly masks during clinical encounters with patients with MRSA infection. Infection control may also include keeping patients in isolated rooms or in the same rooms as other patients with MRSA.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: MRSA remains a major public health challenge, reflecting decades of bacterial adaptation and shifting epidemiology. Since its identification in 1961, MRSA has evolved from a predominantly hospital-acquired pathogen to one that also thrives in community settings. Despite progress in infection control, the persistence of MRSA colonization and transmission underscores the ongoing need for vigilance, prevention, and evidence-based management strategies to reduce morbidity and mortality.

title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective MRSA management relies on a coordinated, interprofessional approach. Physicians, advanced practitioners, and nurses must recognize infection patterns, implement screening protocols, and ensure timely isolation and treatment. Pharmacists play a key role in antibiotic stewardship by optimizing therapy based on culture results and minimizing the development of resistance. Infection control specialists guide adherence to hygiene standards and surveillance. Open communication, shared decision-making, and consistent education among healthcare professionals strengthen patient-centered care, improve safety, and sustain progress in controlling MRSA transmission within healthcare and community environments.
